title: Working out the payback on an AI phone host
seoTitle: ROI for an AI phone host in restaurants | ROAL
description: Estimate restaurant ROI for an AI phone host with order volume, labor savings, and fees, using simple math owners can plug in.
question: How do I figure out the roi of an AI phone host for my restaurant?
answer: Start with your average order size, how many calls turn into orders, and what you spend now on missed calls, phone labor, or delivery app commissions. With ROAL, the cost is $0.90 per completed phone order and there is no monthly fee, so the payback usually comes down to whether those orders are cheaper than your current phone setup or lost sales.
summary: You’ll learn a simple way to compare an AI phone host cost against your current phone costs and order volume.
intro:
An AI phone host pays off when it helps capture more phone orders for less than you already spend to answer the phone. For a restaurant owner, the real question is not whether it sounds modern. It is whether the numbers make sense on a normal week.

The easiest way to judge roi ai phone restaurant math is to compare your current cost per order with the cost of a confirmed order through ROAL. Since ROAL charges $0.90 per completed phone order and has no monthly fee, the math is straightforward: plug in your own order count, average ticket, and current phone costs, then see where the break-even point lands.

sections.h2: What should I count when I compare phone costs?
sections.body:
Start with the costs that touch your phone line today. Do not guess at fancy savings. Use the real pieces you can see on a weekly or monthly basis.

Here is the basic checklist:
- Orders that come in by phone now
- Calls that go to voicemail or get missed during rushes
- Time your staff spends answering simple questions like hours, address, parking, and menu items
- Money spent on human answering services or phone staff
- Money lost to delivery apps when a phone order gets placed there instead

A simple owner script can help you track the right calls: "Is this a pickup order or delivery? What is the name and phone number?" If your team is already saying that 40 times on a Friday, those calls have a cost, even before you count the order.

If you want a fast starting point, use [the phone host cost calculator](/tools/phone-host-cost-calculator) and compare it with your current setup. Keep the math in one place so you can swap in your own numbers later.

sections.h2: How do I calculate payback with simple restaurant numbers?
sections.body:
Use a plain worked example, then replace the numbers with yours. Say your restaurant gets 300 completed phone orders in a month and your average order is $28. That is $8,400 in phone-order sales.

Now compare two common setups:

| Setup | Example cost formula | Example monthly cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ROAL | 300 completed orders x $0.90 | $270 |
| Monthly AI phone plan | fixed fee, often around $79 to $599, whether or not orders come in | $79 to $599 |
| Human answering service | often billed per minute or per call | varies with usage |

ROAL’s cost in this example is tied to completed orders, not empty calls. If your shop has a slow week, you do not pay a flat monthly fee on top of it. If your phone volume is higher, the cost rises with actual completed orders. That makes it easier to line up cost with sales.

To find payback, ask: what are you already spending, or losing, to get those same orders? If your current phone costs are more than $270 for the month, ROAL is cheaper on this example. If not, the next question is whether it frees up staff time or captures orders you would otherwise miss.

sections.h2: Where does the money come back to the restaurant?
sections.body:
Payback does not only come from direct savings. It can also come from better order capture and fewer interruptions at the counter. That matters most for pizza shops, takeout spots, delis, and family restaurants where the phone rings while people are plating food or running tickets.

Use this quick breakdown:
1. A caller asks about hours, parking, or the menu.
2. ROAL answers from your live menu and public info.
3. If the caller wants pickup or delivery, it takes the order, name, phone number, items, sizes, modifiers, and notes.
4. It quotes a ready time and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

That means fewer back-and-forth calls for simple questions and fewer order slips written by hand. It also means the host can hand off harder calls like catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, or manager requests with a summary.

A useful phone line for your staff is: "I’m putting you through for that one." That keeps the front of house focused on service, while the phone host handles the routine work. If your staff is constantly leaving the line to answer the same menu questions, the payback can show up there too.

sections.h2: How do ROAL’s pricing terms change the math?
sections.body:
ROAL uses usage-based pricing that is easy to explain to an owner or bookkeeper: $0.90 per completed phone order, billed monthly. There is no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free.

That matters because many other phone tools in the market charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often in the rough range of $79 to $599, whether or not orders come in. Human answering services are often billed by the minute or by the call. With ROAL, you only pay when the order is confirmed and the ticket reaches the kitchen screen.

Here is a quick plug-in formula:
- Monthly completed phone orders x $0.90 = ROAL cost
- Your current phone labor or service cost = what you are replacing
- Difference = monthly savings or extra cost

For example, if you have 500 completed phone orders in a busy month, the ROAL charge would be $450. Plug in your own order count and compare it with whatever you pay now for staff time, answering service invoices, or other phone costs. You can also compare it with [monthly AI phone plan pricing](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans) if you are weighing one pricing model against another.

sections.h2: What setup steps matter before I judge the numbers?
sections.body:
The setup is simple, but it still affects your results. ROAL can build a phone host in about a minute from your website, Google Maps link, or even just your name and city. The owner can test-call it in the browser before going live, with no sign-up needed.

A practical launch checklist:
- Paste your restaurant website, Google Maps link, or name and city at /try
- Review the menu, prices, hours, and address ROAL reads from public pages
- Upload a menu if you want to fill gaps or use a file in any format
- Pick the host’s name and voice
- Claim the host and forward your existing number to the ROAL line
- Decide whether all calls forward, or only calls that are busy or unanswered
- Test the line with a real call and confirm the kitchen ticket looks right

If you want help with the phone side, [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) can help you get started, but always confirm with your carrier and test the setup. Forwarding is something owners often change later, and it can be turned off any time. That flexibility matters when you are trying to judge payback without getting stuck in a long setup.

sections.h2: What should I watch after the first week?
sections.body:
A payback check should not wait until the end of the season. After the first week, look at the calls that came in, the orders that were confirmed, and the questions that got answered without bothering the staff.

Use this short review list:
- How many completed phone orders did you get?
- Did the kitchen screen ticket match what the caller wanted?
- Were sold-out items blocked the right way?
- Which questions landed in the inbox because the host did not know them yet?
- Did callers in another language get through clearly?

ROAL’s dashboard gives you call history with transcripts and recordings, live kitchen tickets, a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus. That helps you spot what is helping and what needs a quick fix. If a question comes up once, you answer it once, and the host knows it from then on.

A real-world owner mindset helps here: don’t ask, "Did it sound perfect?" Ask, "Did it save time or capture an order?" If the answer is yes, the payback is moving in the right direction. If not, update the menu, hours, or FAQs and retest.

sections.h2: When does an AI phone host make the most sense?
sections.body:
The strongest payback usually comes in restaurants where the phone rings during service and the staff is already busy. That includes pizza shops, takeout counters, delis, family restaurants, and any place with lots of repeat questions about the menu, hours, address, or parking.

It can also make sense when:
- You get a lot of pickup or delivery calls
- Staff keep getting pulled off the line during rushes
- You have more than one location and need each one to handle calls cleanly
- You want to reduce the chance of a caller giving up after hearing voicemail
- You want a cleaner handoff for catering, allergy-sensitive questions, or reservation requests

ROAL is pre-launch, so it is smart to judge it on your own numbers rather than promises. Built by Venkata Vamsi in Jersey City, NJ, it started with nearby restaurants and works for any US restaurant. If you want a simple first step, [build a free test host](/try) from your website, then call it yourself and see how it handles your menu and hours.

A good final question is: "Would I rather pay a fixed fee even on a slow month, or pay only for confirmed phone orders?" That answer is where the payback usually becomes clear.

faq.q: How do I calculate ROI for an AI phone host at my restaurant?
faq.a: Start with your monthly completed phone orders, your average order size, and what you spend now on phone labor, answering services, or lost orders. Then compare that total with $0.90 per completed order for ROAL. The break-even point is where your current phone costs are higher than the AI phone host cost.

faq.q: Is pay-per-order cheaper than a monthly AI phone plan?
faq.a: It depends on how many orders you actually take by phone. If your volume is uneven, pay-per-order can be easier to justify because you only pay when a ticket reaches the kitchen screen. Fixed monthly plans can still make sense for some shops, but they cost the same even in slower periods.

faq.q: Does an AI phone host replace my staff on the phone?
faq.a: It can take routine calls, pickup and delivery orders, and common questions about hours, address, parking, and the menu. It should not handle card numbers, and it sends tricky calls like catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, or manager requests to staff with a summary. That makes it a tool for the team, not a full replacement for judgment calls.

faq.q: How do I know if the payback is good enough for my restaurant?
faq.a: Look at the first month of completed orders and compare the cost to what you would have paid another way. If you are replacing missed calls, a costly fixed plan, or staff time spent on repetitive phone work, the payback may show up quickly. The best test is to plug in your own order count and average ticket, not a generic industry number.
